newsitem.title: USA: Objections mount to Leach's U.S. banking package.
newsitem.headline: Objections mount to Leach's U.S. banking package.

text.p: Objections mounted Thursday to a package of banking legislation that includes measures to shore up the thrift industry insurance fund.

A group of democrats led by Joe Kennedy (D-Mass.) said they want further changes to the bill's community reinvestment act provisions and Comptroller of the Currency Eugene Ludwig said the plan would hurt banks who want to sell insurance.

House Banking Committee Chairman Jim Leach said he still hoped the bill would come before the House next week but it was clear his patience was being strained in trying to balance the demands from all sides.
"I am perplexed and close to astonished that the minority has taken that position," Leach told a meeting of his committee on consumer debt where Kennedy raised the issue.
On Monday, Leach said he believed his proposal would have the support of major banking and insurance groups.
It includes legislation approved by his committee earlier this year to shore up the Savings Association Insurance Fund.

It also includes elements of earlier legislation aimed at modernizing the banking industry and Leach said it would exclude earlier controversial language covering the Community Reinvestment Act and banks' involvement in insurance.
The proposal calls for a General Accounting Office study of state supervision of national bank insurance activities.
To meet objections voiced by Democrats, it scales back earlier proposals to cut regulatory red tape for banks.
Ludwig, whose office regulates nationally chartered banks, told the hearing he opposed the provisions.
"Although you've worked very diligently on those provisions, they would materially hurt banks that want to sell insurance and could roll back the clock in this area," Ludwig said.
Separately the American Bankers Association released a letter to Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin in which it expressed grave concern at the direction the legislative measure appeared to be heading.
The ABA feared the bill would ultimately have no limits on thrifts transferring to the better funded Bank Insurance Fund, thereby further undermining the thrift insurance fund.
Such a bill "we would have to strongly oppose," ABA said.
The banking industry group also expressed concern about negotiations between Democrats and Republicans on the regulatory relief provisions that had already been weakened from their original versions.
